meanings.short: Of a complex matrix or operator: keeping every length and every angle between vectors; a unitary matrix has perpendicular unit columns.
meanings.long: A unitary matrix U satisfies U*U = I, where U* is the conjugate transpose, so its inverse is its conjugate transpose. In quantum mechanics unitary operators describe changes, such as time evolution, that keep total probability equal to one.

meanings.short: A set of independent vectors from which every vector in a space can be built, in exactly one way, as a combination.
meanings.long: The number of vectors in a basis is the dimension of the space. The same space has many bases; the components of a vector depend on which basis is used.

origin: Latin spectrum, an appearance or image.

meanings.short: The spread of light or other radiation over its wavelengths, or the full set of values a quantity such as energy can take.
meanings.long: A prism spreads white light into its spectrum of colours; a hot body gives a smooth spectrum, a thin gas bright or dark lines. In quantum mechanics the spectrum of a system is its set of allowed energies.

meanings.short: The set of eigenvalues of a matrix.
meanings.long: The name comes from light being split into pure colours, as a matrix is split into its eigenvalues and eigenvectors; the spectral theorem describes this for symmetric matrices.

meanings.short: Changing sign when two things are swapped, or when a shape or function is reflected; an antisymmetric matrix equals minus its transpose.
meanings.long: A matrix A is antisymmetric (skew-symmetric) when its transpose is −A; its diagonal is zero and its eigenvalues are purely imaginary (or zero). A wavefunction of identical fermions is antisymmetric: swapping two particles changes its sign.

meanings.short: All the vectors made by combining the columns of a matrix; Ax = b can be solved exactly when b lies in it.
meanings.long: The column space of A is the set of all Ax. It is a subspace whose dimension is the rank of A, and the pivot columns form a basis for it.

meanings.short: Of a set of vectors: each has length one and each is at right angles to all the others.
meanings.long: In an orthonormal basis the component of a vector along each basis vector is just a dot product, which makes calculations simple. The columns of an orthogonal or unitary matrix are orthonormal.

meanings.short: The number of independent directions in a space: one for a line, two for a plane, three for ordinary space.
meanings.long: A line has one dimension, a plane two. In physics the word also has a second use: the dimensions of a quantity are the kinds of unit it is built from, such as length divided by time for a speed.

meanings.short: The number of vectors in any basis of a vector space or subspace.
meanings.long: Every basis of a space has the same number of vectors, and that number is its dimension. The column space and the row space of a matrix both have dimension equal to its rank.

meanings.short: The kind of unit a quantity is measured in, such as length, or length divided by time for a speed.
meanings.long: Checking that both sides of an equation have the same dimensions catches many mistakes.

meanings.short: A measured size of an object, such as its length, width or height.
An oval curve: the set of points whose distances from two fixed points, the foci, add up to the same total.
meanings.long: A circle is the special ellipse with both foci at the centre. Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at one focus, and the level curves of a positive definite quadratic form are ellipses.

meanings.short: A closed surface like a ball stretched or squashed along three perpendicular directions; every flat slice through it is an ellipse.
meanings.long: A sphere stretched by different amounts along three perpendicular axes is an ellipsoid. The surface xᵀAx = 1 is an ellipsoid when A is positive definite, with axes along the eigenvectors of A.

meanings.short: An open curve with two separate branches: the set of points whose distances from two fixed points differ by the same amount.
meanings.long: The curve xy = 1 is a hyperbola. A quadratic form with one positive and one negative eigenvalue has hyperbolas as its level curves.

meanings.short: Of a square matrix or operator: having an inverse that undoes it; for a matrix this happens exactly when its determinant is not zero.
meanings.long: An invertible n × n matrix has n pivots, independent columns and only the zero vector in its nullspace, and Ax = b has exactly one solution for every b.

meanings.short: Of a square matrix: invertible, with a determinant that is not zero.
meanings.long: Non-singular and invertible mean the same thing. Elimination on a non-singular matrix finds a full set of pivots.

everyday: Not the grammatical singular or 'remarkable': in maths and physics it means something breaks down.

meanings.short: Breaking down at a point: a quantity becomes infinite or undefined there.
meanings.long: A density that grows without limit at the centre, or a coordinate system that fails at a horizon, is called singular there. A singularity may be real, or only an artefact of the coordinates.

meanings.short: Of a square matrix: having no inverse, because its determinant is zero and some nonzero vector is sent to zero.
meanings.long: A singular matrix has dependent columns and a nullspace with more than the zero vector, so Ax = b has either no solution or infinitely many.

meanings.short: All the vectors x that a matrix sends to zero, that is, all solutions of Ax = 0.
meanings.long: The nullspace of an m × n matrix is a subspace of n-dimensional space, of dimension n minus the rank. The special solutions form a basis for it.

meanings.short: In elimination, the first nonzero number in a row, used to clear out the entries below it.
meanings.long: Elimination divides by the pivots, so a zero in a pivot position needs a row exchange, and if none helps the matrix is singular. The number of pivots is the rank; for a symmetric matrix, all pivots positive means positive definite.

meanings.short: A column of a matrix that contains a pivot after elimination; the matching columns of the original matrix form a basis for its column space.
An unknown whose column has a pivot; once the free variables are chosen, the pivot variables are found by back substitution.
An unknown whose column has no pivot, so it can be given any value; the other unknowns are then fixed by the equations.
meanings.long: Each free variable of Ax = 0 gives one special solution, so the number of free variables is the dimension of the nullspace.

meanings.short: A column of a matrix with no pivot after elimination; it is a combination of the pivot columns before it.
All the vectors that can be made by combining the rows of a matrix; it is the column space of its transpose.
meanings.long: Its dimension is the rank, the same as that of the column space. The row space is at right angles to the nullspace.

meanings.short: The nullspace of the transpose of a matrix: all the combinations of its rows that give zero.
meanings.long: It holds the vectors y with yᵀA = 0. It is at right angles to the column space, and its dimension is the number of rows minus the rank. It records which combinations of the rows give zero.

meanings.short: The column space, nullspace, row space and left nullspace of a matrix, whose dimensions are all fixed by its rank.
meanings.long: For an m × n matrix of rank r, the row space and column space have dimension r, the nullspace n − r and the left nullspace m − r. The row space is perpendicular to the nullspace, and the column space to the left nullspace.

everyday: Not 'alike' in a loose sense: similar matrices are related by a precise change of basis.

meanings.short: Of two square matrices: describing the same transformation in two different bases.
meanings.long: A and B are similar when B = M⁻¹AM for some invertible M. Similar matrices have the same eigenvalues, the same determinant and the same number of independent eigenvectors. Every matrix is similar to a Jordan form.

meanings.short: A matrix with an extra column, the right-hand side b, added to it, so that elimination works on the equations and b together.
In a graph or network, a connection between two nodes, drawn as a line or an arrow.
meanings.long: In the incidence matrix of a graph each edge gives one row, with −1 where the edge starts and +1 where it ends.

meanings.short: Solving equations by subtracting multiples of one from another until each unknown can be found in turn.
meanings.long: Gaussian elimination turns a matrix into an upper triangular one, row by row, using the pivots; back substitution then solves the equations from the bottom up. It is how computers solve most systems of linear equations.

meanings.short: Swapping two rows of a matrix, needed in elimination when a zero sits where a pivot should be.
meanings.long: A row exchange is done by multiplying by a permutation matrix. Each exchange changes the sign of the determinant.

meanings.short: The rule that the current through a conductor equals the voltage across it divided by its resistance.
meanings.long: It holds well for metals at a steady temperature; resistance is measured in ohms. In a network each edge obeys Ohm's law: its current is its conductance times the potential difference across it.

meanings.short: A rearrangement of a list of things into a new order.
meanings.long: Three objects have six permutations. A permutation is even or odd according to whether it takes an even or odd number of swaps, which sets the sign of its term in the determinant.

meanings.short: A matrix made by reordering the rows of the identity matrix; multiplying by it reorders the rows of another matrix the same way.
meanings.long: Each row and each column has a single 1. The inverse of a permutation matrix is its transpose, and its determinant is +1 or −1.

meanings.short: The theorem that every real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors, so a turn of the axes makes it diagonal.
meanings.long: In matrix form, a symmetric A equals QΛQᵀ with Q orthogonal. The new axes, along the eigenvectors, are the principal axes of the ellipse or ellipsoid that A describes.

meanings.short: The theorem that a symmetric (or Hermitian) matrix has real eigenvalues and a full set of perpendicular eigenvectors.
meanings.long: It means such a matrix can be written as a sum of its eigenvalues times projections onto its eigenvectors. In quantum mechanics it guarantees that measurable quantities have real values and a complete set of states.

meanings.short: The theorem that an operator has a full set of perpendicular unit eigenvectors exactly when it commutes with its adjoint, as Hermitian operators do.
The shadow of a vector on a line or plane: the nearest point to it there, found by dropping a perpendicular.
meanings.long: The projection of b onto the line through a is (aᵀb/aᵀa) a. The part of b left over is perpendicular to the line or plane, which is what makes the projection the closest point.

meanings.short: An image thrown onto a screen by a lens or a beam of light.
A quantity added up along the line of sight, giving a flat map of something spread through space.
A matrix that sends every vector to its projection onto a fixed line, plane or subspace.
meanings.long: Projecting onto the column space of A uses P = A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ. A projection matrix is symmetric and projecting twice changes nothing, so P² = P.

meanings.short: The number of independent columns of a matrix, which always equals the number of independent rows.
meanings.long: The rank is the number of pivots found by elimination and the dimension of the column space and of the row space. An n × n matrix is invertible exactly when its rank is n.

meanings.short: Of a tensor: the number of indices it carries, such as one for a vector and two for a matrix-like tensor.
Of a matrix: having rank as large as its size allows; full column rank means independent columns, full row rank independent rows.
meanings.long: With full column rank, Ax = b has at most one solution; with full row rank, it has at least one for every b. A square matrix of full rank is invertible.

meanings.short: Of a matrix: having rank exactly one, so it is a column times a row and every column is a multiple of one column.
The span of some vectors is everything that can be made by combining them; vectors span a space when they fill all of it.
meanings.long: The span of two independent vectors in three dimensions is a plane through the origin. A basis is a set of vectors that spans the space and is independent.

meanings.short: To stretch across or cover a range.
A solution of Ax = 0 found by setting one free variable to 1 and the others to 0; together they build every solution.
meanings.long: There is one special solution for each free variable, and every solution of Ax = 0 is a combination of them, so they form a basis for the nullspace.

meanings.short: Whether a state or solution returns after a small disturbance (stable) or moves further and further from it (unstable).
meanings.long: For du/dt = Au, solutions die away when every eigenvalue of A has a negative real part. In mechanics an equilibrium is stable at a minimum of the potential energy.

meanings.short: A set of vectors inside a larger space that is a space itself: sums and multiples of its vectors stay inside it.
meanings.long: Every subspace contains the zero vector. In three dimensions the subspaces are the origin, lines and planes through it, and the whole space.

meanings.short: The set made of everything that is in one set or the other, or both.
meanings.long: The union of two subspaces is usually not a subspace, because the sum of a vector from each can land outside both.

meanings.short: The set made of everything that is in one set or the other, or both.
The part common to two or more sets or shapes: everything that belongs to all of them.
meanings.long: Two planes through the origin usually intersect in a line. The intersection of two subspaces is always a subspace.

meanings.short: A square matrix with only zeros below its diagonal (upper triangular) or only zeros above it (lower triangular).
meanings.long: Its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries, and those entries are its eigenvalues. Elimination turns a matrix into an upper triangular one, which back substitution then solves.

meanings.short: A square matrix with only zeros below its diagonal, or only zeros above it.
How many times an eigenvalue is repeated as a root of the characteristic polynomial.
meanings.long: It is at least as large as the geometric multiplicity. When it is larger, the matrix has too few independent eigenvectors to be diagonalised.

meanings.short: How many independent eigenvectors belong to one eigenvalue.
meanings.long: It equals the dimension of the nullspace of A − λI. A matrix can be diagonalised exactly when, for every eigenvalue, it equals the algebraic multiplicity.

meanings.short: The rule that grouping does not matter: when three things are combined, which pair is combined first makes no difference.
meanings.long: For numbers, (a + b) + c = a + (b + c); for matrices, (AB)C = A(BC). Matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative: AB and BA usually differ.

meanings.short: Describing the same vectors, or the same transformation, with a different set of basis vectors.
meanings.long: If the columns of M are the new basis vectors, a transformation with matrix A in the old basis has matrix M⁻¹AM in the new one. A good basis, such as the eigenvectors, makes the matrix simple.

meanings.short: The matrix of the numbers that multiply the unknowns in a system of linear equations.
The square array of the numbers that multiply each product of basis states in a state of two particles.
Seeing a system of linear equations as lines, planes or higher-dimensional planes, one per equation, that meet at the solution.
Seeing a system Ax = b as the question of which combination of the columns of A gives b.
Of vectors: none of them is a combination of the others, so the only combination giving zero uses all zero coefficients.
meanings.long: Independent vectors point in genuinely different directions. The columns of a matrix are independent exactly when its nullspace contains only the zero vector.

meanings.short: Of random quantities or events: knowing one tells you nothing about the other, so their joint probability is the product of their separate probabilities.
Of random quantities or events: knowing one tells you nothing about the other, so their joint probability is the product of their separate probabilities.
The property of a set of vectors that none of them can be built as a combination of the others.
meanings.long: Vectors are linearly dependent when some combination of them, not all coefficients zero, gives the zero vector.

meanings.short: To rewrite a matrix in a basis of its eigenvectors, where it becomes diagonal, with its eigenvalues down the diagonal.
meanings.long: If A has n independent eigenvectors, the columns of S, then S⁻¹AS = Λ is diagonal, so A = SΛS⁻¹ and powers of A are easy: Aᵏ = SΛᵏS⁻¹. Matrices without enough eigenvectors cannot be diagonalised.

meanings.short: In a square matrix, the entries running from the top left corner to the bottom right; a diagonal matrix has zeros everywhere else.
meanings.long: Multiplying by a diagonal matrix simply stretches each coordinate by its own factor. Its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, and a matrix with enough eigenvectors can be diagonalised.

meanings.short: In a square matrix, the entries running from the top left corner to the bottom right; a diagonal matrix has zeros everywhere else.
A line running at 45° between two perpendicular axes.
The staircase shape a matrix takes after elimination: each row's first nonzero entry, its pivot, lies to the right of the one above.
meanings.long: In reduced row echelon form every pivot is 1 and is the only nonzero entry in its column. From it the special solutions can be read off directly.

meanings.short: A matrix that carries out one step of elimination, subtracting a multiple of one row from another, when it multiplies a matrix.
meanings.long: It is the identity matrix with one extra entry below the diagonal. Its inverse adds the row back.

meanings.short: The set with nothing in it.
meanings.long: It is not a vector space, since every vector space must contain the zero vector.

meanings.short: The formula linking the exponential function to sines and cosines: e to the power iθ equals cos θ plus i sin θ.
meanings.long: It shows that e^(iθ) is a point on the unit circle at angle θ, which makes complex exponentials the natural way to handle oscillations and waves.

meanings.short: For a connected graph: the number of nodes, minus the number of edges, plus the number of independent loops equals 1.
meanings.long: It follows from the dimensions of the four subspaces of the incidence matrix.

meanings.short: Writing something, such as a number, a matrix or an operator, as a product of simpler pieces.
meanings.long: For matrices, each factorization records a method: A = LU records elimination, A = QR the Gram–Schmidt process, and A = SΛS⁻¹ the eigenvectors.

meanings.short: A fast method for multiplying by the Fourier matrix, splitting the work in halves again and again, so n log n steps replace n².
meanings.long: Published by Cooley and Tukey in 1965, it made signal and image processing practical. For n = 1024 it needs about five thousand multiplications instead of a million.

meanings.short: Short for fast Fourier transform, a quick method for computing a discrete Fourier transform.
The square matrix whose entries are powers of a complex root of one, used to change a signal into its frequencies and back.
meanings.long: Its columns are orthogonal, so its inverse is simply its conjugate transpose divided by n. The fast Fourier transform multiplies by it quickly.

meanings.short: A way of writing a repeating function as a sum of sines and cosines whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of one frequency.
meanings.long: Each coefficient is found by multiplying by the matching sine or cosine and integrating over one period, because these functions are orthogonal. Fourier series are the infinite-dimensional version of writing a vector in an orthogonal basis.

meanings.short: A method that continues elimination upwards as well as downwards until the matrix becomes the identity, which finds the inverse.
meanings.long: Applied to the augmented matrix [A I], it ends with [I A⁻¹]. It also gives the reduced row echelon form.

meanings.short: Connected to the earth, or to a point held at zero potential, so the potential there is fixed at zero.
meanings.long: A grounded conductor can exchange charge with the earth freely. Grounding one node of a network removes the freedom to add a constant to all the potentials, which makes the equations solvable.

meanings.short: A square matrix whose entries are all +1 or −1 and whose columns are perpendicular to each other.
The matrix of a graph, with one row for each edge and one column for each node, recording where each edge starts and ends.
meanings.long: Each row has −1 at the node where its edge starts and +1 where it ends. Its nullspace, column space and left nullspace describe constant potentials, voltage differences and currents around loops.

meanings.short: A square matrix with one eigenvalue repeated down its diagonal, ones just above the diagonal and zeros elsewhere; it has only one eigenvector.
The simplest matrix similar to a given one: Jordan blocks along the diagonal, one block for each independent eigenvector.
meanings.long: Every square matrix is similar to a Jordan matrix. When there are enough eigenvectors all blocks are 1 × 1 and the Jordan form is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues.

meanings.short: The rule that at any junction of a circuit or network, the total current flowing in equals the total flowing out.
meanings.long: It expresses conservation of charge. For a network with incidence matrix A, the currents y obey Aᵀy = 0.

meanings.short: A sum of vectors, each first multiplied by a number, such as 3u + 2v.
meanings.long: Ax is the linear combination of the columns of A with the entries of x as the multipliers.

meanings.short: Fitting a straight line, or a combination of chosen functions, to data points, usually by least squares.
A way to fit a model to data by choosing it to make the sum of the squared errors as small as possible.
meanings.long: For Ax = b with no exact solution, the least-squares solution x̂ solves the normal equations AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb, and Ax̂ is the projection of b onto the column space of A.

everyday: Not 'ordinary': normal here means at right angles, because the error is perpendicular to the columns.

meanings.short: The equations whose solution gives the least-squares best fit, found by making the error perpendicular to every column.
meanings.long: For Ax = b they read AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb. They say that the error b − Ax̂ is perpendicular to every column of A; 'normal' here means at right angles.

meanings.short: In a graph or network, a closed path of edges that returns to where it started.
meanings.long: Each independent loop gives a dependency among the rows of the incidence matrix. A graph without loops is a tree.

meanings.short: A graph that connects all its nodes without any loop.
meanings.long: A tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges. In an incidence matrix, the edges of a tree give independent rows.

meanings.short: Of a matrix: having mostly zero entries, so it can be stored and used much faster than a full one.
Of compression: making data smaller in a way that can be undone exactly, with nothing lost.
Of compression: making data much smaller by throwing away details the eye or ear hardly notices, so the original cannot be recovered exactly.
meanings.long: JPEG images use lossy compression: they keep the large coefficients in a good basis and drop the small ones.

meanings.short: A square matrix with no negative entries whose columns each add up to one; it moves probabilities or populations from one step to the next.
meanings.long: Every Markov matrix has the eigenvalue 1, and when all its entries are positive the other eigenvalues are smaller than 1 in size, so repeated steps approach a steady state.

meanings.short: A square matrix whose columns are perpendicular unit vectors; it rotates or reflects without changing lengths, and its inverse is its transpose.
meanings.long: Q is orthogonal when QᵀQ = I. Orthogonal matrices make projections and least squares simple, and their determinant is +1 or −1.

meanings.short: A step-by-step method that turns independent vectors into perpendicular unit vectors that span the same space.
meanings.long: Each new vector has its parts along the earlier ones subtracted, then is divided by its length. Written as matrices, the method gives A = QR.

meanings.short: A data point far from the pattern of the others, often from a mistake, which can pull a least-squares fit badly off.
Of a symmetric matrix or quadratic form: always giving a positive value for any nonzero input; equivalently, all its eigenvalues are positive.
meanings.long: In symbols, xᵀAx > 0 for every nonzero x. Equivalent tests are all pivots positive or all upper-left determinants positive. The graph of xᵀAx is then a bowl with its minimum at the origin, and xᵀAx = 1 is an ellipse or ellipsoid.

meanings.short: Of a metric: giving every nonzero step a positive squared length, as in ordinary space; the metric of spacetime is not.
Of a symmetric matrix: xᵀAx is never negative; all its eigenvalues are positive or zero.
The nearest thing to an inverse for a matrix with none: it carries outputs back to their starting points and sends everything else to zero.
meanings.long: Written A⁺, it maps the column space back to the row space and sends the left nullspace to zero. It can be built from the singular value decomposition by inverting the nonzero singular values. For an invertible matrix it is the ordinary inverse.

meanings.short: An expression in which every term has degree two, such as ax² + 2bxy + cy², written xᵀAx with a symmetric matrix A.
meanings.long: Near a critical point a function looks like a quadratic form, and whether A is positive definite decides whether the point is a minimum.

meanings.short: A rule giving each term from the ones before it, or a method that solves a problem by applying itself to smaller copies of it.
meanings.long: Recursion relations give, for example, the coefficients of a series solution one after another. The fast Fourier transform is recursive: a transform of size n is built from two of size n/2, and so on down to size 1.

meanings.short: Writing any matrix as A = UΣVᵀ: a rotation (perhaps with a reflection), a stretching along perpendicular axes, and another rotation.
meanings.long: U and V are orthogonal and Σ is diagonal, holding the singular values. It works for every matrix, square or not, and gives orthonormal bases for all four fundamental subspaces.

meanings.short: Short for singular value decomposition, which writes any matrix as a rotation, a stretching and another rotation (reflections allowed).
One of the stretching factors of a matrix in its singular value decomposition; the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA.
meanings.long: Singular values are never negative, and the number of nonzero ones is the rank. The largest one is the most any vector's length can be multiplied by.

meanings.short: The basis made of the columns of the identity matrix: vectors with a single 1 and zeros elsewhere.
Setting all coefficients smaller than a chosen size to zero, so only the important ones are kept.
A collection of objects, called vectors, that can be added together and multiplied by numbers, with the results staying in the collection.
meanings.long: Arrows in the plane, lists of n numbers, matrices of one size and functions can all form vector spaces. Every vector space contains a zero vector.

meanings.short: A small wave; in optics, one of the little spherical waves that, by Huygens' idea, spread out from every point of a wavefront.
meanings.long: Adding up all the wavelets from one wavefront gives the next wavefront. The idea explains refraction and diffraction.

meanings.short: One of a set of short, localised wave shapes used as a basis for signals and images, made by shifting and squeezing one basic shape.
meanings.long: A wavelet basis describes a signal piece by piece, so sharp edges in an image need only a few coefficients; this makes wavelets good for compression.

meanings.short: The vector whose components are all zero; adding it to any vector changes nothing.
Solving a triangular system from the bottom up: the last equation gives the last unknown, which is put into the one above, and so on.
The factorization A = LU of a matrix into a lower triangular L, which records the elimination steps, times the upper triangular U it produces.
A large network in which any two points are joined by a short chain of links, thanks to a few long shortcuts.
meanings.long: The popular 'six degrees of separation' between any two people is the classic example.

meanings.short: For a complex number a + bi, the ordinary number a.
meanings.long: The other part, b, is the imaginary part. The real part of e^(λt) decides whether it grows or decays: it grows when λ has a positive real part and decays when the real part is negative.

meanings.short: Of a root of one: a complex number whose powers give every other root of the same order before coming back to 1.
A collection of matrices, or other objects, in which the product of any two and the inverse of each are again in the collection.
meanings.long: The invertible matrices form a group, and so do the permutation matrices and the orthogonal matrices.

meanings.short: The longest diameter of an ellipse or ellipsoid: the line through its centre along which it is widest.
meanings.long: Half of it is the semi-major axis. A circular disc seen tilted on the sky looks like an ellipse whose major axis keeps the disc's full width, while the minor axis is shortened by the tilt.

meanings.short: The shortest diameter of an ellipse or ellipsoid: the line through its centre along which it is narrowest.
meanings.long: For the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with a > b, the major axis has length 2a and the minor axis 2b, at right angles to each other. An ellipsoid with three different axes also has a middle one between them.
